pests.name: Scale insects
pests.description: Attached bumps on stems or leaves may accompany poor growth or honeydew. Check: Check whether bumps are insects and identify the scale type. First actions: Remove small infestations gently where appropriate; conserve predators and seek species-specific advice. Similar-looking problems: Plant tissue; mealybugs; other insects. These signs suggest possibilities, not a confirmed diagnosis.

pests.name: Caterpillars
pests.description: Chewed leaves, holes and droppings can accompany caterpillars. Check: Inspect both surfaces and nearby shelter; identify the caterpillar and host. First actions: Hand-pick where practical and use suitable exclusion; distinguish pest species from desirable butterflies. Similar-looking problems: Slugs; beetles; other chewing pests. These signs suggest possibilities, not a confirmed diagnosis.

pests.name: Spider mites
pests.description: Fine stippling and sometimes delicate webbing, often in warm dry conditions. Check: Use a hand lens on leaf undersides; confirm mites before treatment. First actions: Reduce plant stress and conserve predators; use suitable controls only after identification. Similar-looking problems: Thrips; nutrient problems. These signs suggest possibilities, not a confirmed diagnosis.

pests.name: Slugs and snails
pests.description: Night-feeding molluscs that chew irregular holes in seedlings and soft foliage and may leave silvery trails.

pests.name: Thrips
pests.description: Silvery scarring or distorted growth may accompany tiny slender insects. Check: Inspect flowers and leaves with a hand lens; look for insects and dark waste spots. First actions: Monitor and remove badly affected material; conserve beneficial insects. Similar-looking problems: Spider mites; wind damage. These signs suggest possibilities, not a confirmed diagnosis.

pests.name: Whitefly
pests.description: Small pale flying insects beneath leaves; honeydew may occur. Check: Inspect undersides and gently disturb foliage to check for adults. First actions: Monitor regularly; encourage beneficial insects and use host-appropriate controls. Similar-looking problems: Aphids; scale; leaf debris. These signs suggest possibilities, not a confirmed diagnosis.

pests.name: Aphids
pests.description: Small sap-sucking insects that gather on tender shoots and beneath leaves, sometimes causing curled growth and sticky honeydew.

diseases.name: Powdery mildew
diseases.description: A fungal disease recognised by white or grey powdery patches on leaves and stems; airflow and spacing help reduce it.

diseases.name: Downy mildew
diseases.description: Angular yellow patches and growth beneath leaves may occur; appearance varies by host. Check: Inspect both leaf surfaces and identify the host before choosing management. First actions: Reduce prolonged leaf wetness, improve spacing and remove badly affected material. Similar-looking problems: Powdery mildew; nutrient problems. These signs suggest possibilities, not a confirmed diagnosis.

diseases.name: Tomato early blight
diseases.description: Brown leaf spots with concentric rings can develop, often on older tomato leaves. Check: Inspect spot patterns and compare a tomato-specific reference; do not identify from yellowing alone. First actions: Remove affected debris, reduce soil splash and provide spacing and crop rotation. Similar-looking problems: Septoria leaf spot; other blights; nutrient problems. These signs suggest possibilities, not a confirmed diagnosis.

diseases.name: Grey mould
diseases.description: Grey fuzzy growth and decay can affect flowers, leaves and fruit. Check: Check damaged tissue and persistently damp areas; confirm the host and pattern. First actions: Remove decaying material, improve airflow and avoid prolonged wet foliage. Similar-looking problems: Other rots; ageing flowers. These signs suggest possibilities, not a confirmed diagnosis.

diseases.name: Root rot
diseases.description: Poor growth and wilting can accompany discoloured, decaying roots. Check: Check drainage and roots where this can be done without serious damage; symptoms alone cannot identify a pathogen. First actions: Correct drainage and watering; isolate affected pots and seek host-specific guidance. Similar-looking problems: Waterlogging without infection; underwatering. These signs suggest possibilities, not a confirmed diagnosis.

diseases.name: Rust
diseases.description: Raised orange, brown or yellow pustules may appear on leaves. Check: Inspect the underside and check a host-specific rust reference. First actions: Remove heavily affected leaves and improve airflow; avoid spreading infected material. Similar-looking problems: Other leaf spots; insect eggs. These signs suggest possibilities, not a confirmed diagnosis.

diseases.name: Damping-off
diseases.description: Seedlings fail to emerge or collapse with decay near soil level. Check: Inspect the stem base, moisture and whether tissue is rotting or chewed. First actions: Use clean containers and fresh suitable seed compost; provide drainage and avoid crowding. Similar-looking problems: Dry soil; cutworm or slug damage. These signs suggest possibilities, not a confirmed diagnosis.

Scope: General tomato care; named-cultivar traits and exact watering intervals are not verified. Sources checked 20 October 2026. UK/US calendar dates are not Sydney planting dates.

Sunlight: Choose full sun and a sheltered position. [RHS](https://www.rhs.org.uk/vegetables/tomatoes/grow-your-own)

Watering: Keep the root zone evenly moist; water deeply during dry weather. Check containers frequently because they dry faster. Adjust watering to soil moisture, rainfall and heat rather than a fixed weekly schedule. [Maryland Extension](https://www.extension.umd.edu/resource/growing-tomatoes-home-garden)

Fertiliser: Base additional feeding on soil fertility, growth and fruit load. For containers, RHS recommends high-potassium liquid feed every 10–14 days once fruit begins swelling. Follow the product label for dilution; this is not a universal bed-feeding schedule. [RHS](https://www.rhs.org.uk/vegetables/tomatoes/grow-your-own) · [Maryland Extension](https://www.extension.umd.edu/resource/growing-tomatoes-home-garden)

Support: Support tall plants and tie stems loosely. [RHS](https://www.rhs.org.uk/vegetables/tomatoes/grow-your-own)

Pruning: Confirm the growth habit on the packet or label first. When training indeterminate tomatoes as a single cordon, remove side shoots; retain side shoots on determinate bush tomatoes. Do not apply cordon pruning to an unidentified cultivar. [RHS](https://www.rhs.org.uk/vegetables/tomatoes/grow-your-own)

Unknowns: A cultivar name, water-needs category or heavy-feeder label alone does not establish watering frequency, fertiliser dose or pruning method.
plant_references.management_notes:
Prevention: Water at soil level, maintain airflow and rotate crops to reduce disease pressure. [Maryland Extension](https://www.extension.umd.edu/resource/growing-tomatoes-home-garden)

Checks: Record which leaves or fruits are affected, spot patterns, moisture conditions and visible pests before selecting a response. Early blight can affect tomato foliage and fruit; a catalogue association is not a diagnosis. [Maryland Extension](https://www.extension.umd.edu/resource/growing-tomatoes-home-garden)

Related reference: [[References/Diseases/Tomato early blight]]. Treatment and cultivar resistance are not established by this care record.

plant_references.sowing_notes: Sydney / warm temperate: sow September–May (Eden mild-climate guide). Sow 0.5–1 cm deep and keep moist; germination can be slow. Calendar refers to seed sowing.
plant_references.care_notes: Sydney / warm-temperate guidance. Grow in sun or partial shade with moist, drained soil. The 30 cm plant / 60 cm row spacing uses the wider end of the supplier range. Add compost; feed only as needed. Planning estimates: in row spacing cm, row spacing cm, feeder type, water needs.
plant_references.management_notes: Protect seedlings from slugs and snails. Allow space and airflow; avoid keeping leaves wet overnight. Feeding and water badges are qualitative care categories, not measured requirements.
plant_references.yield_wording: Harvest outer stems once established, leaving the centre to regrow. Seed-grown plants generally reach first harvest in about 65–135 days. A reliable per-plant weight is not established.
plant_references.uses_notes: Use fresh leaves in salads, sauces and cooked dishes; freeze or dry surplus. Retain a separate plant for flowering or seed if desired.

plant_references.summary: Heat-loving annual vegetable grown for tender immature pods.
plant_references.sowing_notes: Sydney / warm temperate: sow October–December after frost risk, when soil is warm. Sow about 1 cm deep. Calendar and spacing are general okra guidance, not a named-variety trial.
plant_references.care_notes: Sydney / warm-temperate guidance. Use a warm, sunny, drained bed. Space 60 cm apart in rows 120 cm apart, the wider end of general okra guidance. Water steadily; excess nitrogen encourages leaves over pods. Planning estimates: in row spacing cm, row spacing cm, feeder type, water needs.
plant_references.management_notes: Mulch and keep drainage open. Inspect leaf undersides and remove badly affected material after identifying the problem. The light-feeder badge means avoid excessive nitrogen, not omit all fertiliser.
plant_references.yield_wording: Pick tender immature pods frequently before they become fibrous. First picking is generally around 80–98 days from sowing; this is maturity time, not harvest-window length. Yield weight varies.
plant_references.uses_notes: Cook young pods in curries, soups or stews, or roast them. Harvest with care where stems or pods are prickly.

plant_references.summary: Climbing bean with stringless young pods, grown on a sturdy support.
plant_references.sowing_notes: Sydney / warm temperate: direct sow September–January after frost, 2–3 cm deep. A 21-day repeat sowing is an optional planning interval within that season, interpreting guidance to sow every few weeks.
plant_references.care_notes: Sydney / warm-temperate guidance. Install a trellis before sowing. Space plants 20 cm apart in rows 100 cm apart. Keep moist after emergence without waterlogging; avoid excessive nitrogen. Planning estimates: in row spacing cm, succession interval days, water needs.
plant_references.management_notes: Protect seedlings from slugs and snails. Water the soil rather than foliage. Nitrogen fixation depends on compatible soil bacteria and does not guarantee feeding nearby crops.
plant_references.yield_wording: The supplier gives about 80 days to first harvest. Pick young pods regularly for a continuing crop; no reliable kilogram yield per plant is verified.
plant_references.uses_notes: Harvest tender green pods for cooking. Let selected pods mature fully only if saving seed or harvesting dry beans; cook mature beans thoroughly.

plant_references.summary: Climbing bean with scarlet flowers and long pods; can regrow from perennial roots in suitable conditions.
plant_references.sowing_notes: Sydney / warm temperate: sow November–February, interpreting the Australian supplier’s late-spring to late-summer window. Wait for warm soil; hot spells can reduce pod set.
plant_references.care_notes: Sydney / warm-temperate guidance. Provide a strong support and moist, compost-rich soil. The 20 cm plant / 100 cm row spacing and pH 6–7 are general climbing-bean planning targets, not cultivar measurements. Planning estimates: in row spacing cm, row spacing cm, soil ph min, soil ph max, harvest window weeks, water needs.
plant_references.management_notes: Watch for aphids, slugs and snails. Keep roots moist through flowering. Nitrogen fixation relies on soil bacteria; flowering plants may still need potassium, especially in pots.
plant_references.yield_wording: Pick tender pods every few days. Eight weeks is a general runner-bean harvest-window baseline, not a Sydney yield guarantee. Perennial roots may regrow in suitable conditions.
plant_references.uses_notes: Grow for scarlet flowers and edible pods. Cook beans before eating; harvest pods young before strings and mature seeds develop.

Support: Support tall plants and tie stems loosely. [RHS](https://www.rhs.org.uk/vegetables/tomatoes/grow-your-own)

Pruning: Confirm the growth habit on the packet or label first. When training indeterminate tomatoes as a single cordon, remove side shoots; retain side shoots on determinate bush tomatoes. Do not apply cordon pruning to an unidentified cultivar. [RHS](https://www.rhs.org.uk/vegetables/tomatoes/grow-your-own)

Unknowns: A cultivar name, water-needs category or heavy-feeder label alone does not establish watering frequency, fertiliser dose or pruning method.
plant_references.management_notes:
Prevention: Water at soil level, maintain airflow and rotate crops to reduce disease pressure. [Maryland Extension](https://www.extension.umd.edu/resource/growing-tomatoes-home-garden)

Checks: Record which leaves or fruits are affected, spot patterns, moisture conditions and visible pests before selecting a response. Early blight can affect tomato foliage and fruit; a catalogue association is not a diagnosis. [Maryland Extension](https://www.extension.umd.edu/resource/growing-tomatoes-home-garden)

Related reference: [[References/Diseases/Tomato early blight]]. Treatment and cultivar resistance are not established by this care record.
plant_references.yield_wording: Pick ripe fruit as it develops. Generic tomato guidance suggests about 65–90 days from transplanting to first harvest, but Sweet 1000 maturity, crop duration and yield remain unverified.
plant_references.uses_notes: Use ripe tomato fruit fresh or cooked. The record is kept separate from Sweet 100 and Sweet Million; fruit size and flavour are not assumed.

plant_references.summary: Spreading perennial herb also called Vietnamese coriander or rau ram, with aromatic leaves used in cooking.
plant_references.sowing_notes: Sydney / warm temperate: plant rooted cuttings September–February, translating the Australian nursery’s spring/summer propagation guidance. Protect from cold.
plant_references.care_notes: Sydney / warm-temperate guidance. Use a warm, sheltered position with dappled shade and fertile, consistently moist soil. Keep in a container to manage spreading stems. A 45 cm plant / 60 cm row layout is a provisional space allowance. Planning estimates: in row spacing cm, row spacing cm, feeder type, water needs.
plant_references.management_notes: Prevent drying out and keep spreading stems out of neighbouring pots. RHS lists acid, neutral and alkaline soils without a numeric range, so exact pH limits are not invented. Water/feed badges are qualitative.
plant_references.yield_wording: Snip fresh leaves and tender tips once established; allow regrowth between pickings. Repeat harvest depends on warmth and vigour, so a fixed weight or harvest duration is not assigned.
plant_references.uses_notes: Use small amounts of fresh peppery leaves in salads, rice-paper rolls and Vietnamese dishes. This is Persicaria odorata, not a Mentha mint.

plant_references.summary: Vigorous perennial mint grown for aromatic leaves with a chocolate-mint scent.
plant_references.sowing_notes: Sydney / warm temperate: divide or plant September–November or March–April. These months translate spring/early-autumn propagation advice to local seasons. Use divisions or cuttings to retain the cultivar.
plant_references.care_notes: Sydney / warm-temperate guidance. Grow in sun or light shade with moist, drained soil. Keep in a pot or root barrier. Allow 60 cm per plant and 65 cm between rows as a contained-bed planning layout; uncontained roots spread farther. Planning estimates: in row spacing cm, row spacing cm, soil ph min, soil ph max, feeder type, water needs.
plant_references.management_notes: Keep runners contained and avoid overhead watering late in the day. Check for rust and remove affected foliage. pH 6–7.5 is a general herb target, not a measured Chocolate cultivar tolerance.
plant_references.yield_wording: Harvest established shoot tips regularly for regrowth. One contained plant can supply repeated small pickings. No measured per-plant yield or fixed harvest duration is available.
plant_references.uses_notes: Use aromatic leaves in teas, desserts and drinks, fresh or dried. Pinching tips encourages a bushier plant.

plant_references.summary: Chinese green radish, also called Qingluobo or green daikon, has elongated roots with green skin and green flesh; the tip may fade to white. Roots are crisp, with sweetness and variable peppery heat. Specialty Produce describes green daikon as relatively mild, while Gardening Know How describes Qingluobo as spicy with a sweet undertone. Expect flavour to vary with cultivar and growing conditions.
plant_references.sowing_notes: Direct sow for a cool-season crop. Grand Prismatic Seed recommends early spring or late summer sowing and thinning to about 10 cm. Gardening Know How favours autumn sowing for Qingluobo because summer heat can encourage bolting. These seasonal recommendations are general guidance, not a verified Sydney month-by-month calendar.
plant_references.care_notes: Leave enough room for the long roots to develop. The spacing property follows Grand Prismatic Seed's 4-inch thinning recommendation, rounded to 10 cm. Other numeric growing requirements remain unverified.
plant_references.management_notes: Watch for premature flowering in hot weather; bolting redirects growth away from the edible root. If buying the treated Qingluobo seed listing supplied by the user, follow the packet's handling instructions.
plant_references.yield_wording: Gardening Know How reports approximately 60 days from seed to maturity; actual timing depends on cultivar and conditions. Its reported root length is roughly 15–30 cm. The user's ABSeeds excerpt gives 12–25 cm; that product page was not independently retrieved.
plant_references.uses_notes: Slice or grate raw for salads, pickle, or cook. The green flesh adds colour to raw dishes. Gardening Know How also describes the leaves as edible and peppery.

ailments.name: Powdery mildew
ailments.description: A fungal disease recognised by white or grey powdery patches on leaves and stems; airflow and spacing help reduce it.
ailments.signs: White or grey powdery patches; severely affected leaves may yellow or distort.
ailments.checks: Inspect both leaf surfaces and confirm the host-specific problem before treatment.
ailments.actions: Improve spacing and airflow, remove badly affected material and choose resistant varieties when available. Companion planting does not cure this disease.

ailments.name: Aphids
ailments.description: Small sap-sucking insects that gather on tender shoots and beneath leaves, sometimes causing curled growth and sticky honeydew.
ailments.signs: Clusters of small insects on tender growth, curled leaves and sticky honeydew.
ailments.checks: Check fresh growth and both leaf surfaces; identify the insects before treatment.
ailments.actions: Dislodge small colonies with a suitable water spray and encourage beneficial insects. Monitor fresh growth.

ailments.name: Slugs and snails
ailments.description: Night-feeding molluscs that chew irregular holes in seedlings and soft foliage and may leave silvery trails.
ailments.signs: Irregular holes, rasped leaf edges and silvery trails, especially after rain.
ailments.checks: Inspect after dark or early morning and distinguish mollusc damage from caterpillar feeding.
ailments.actions: Protect seedlings, remove nearby hiding places and use suitable barriers or direct controls. No companion plant reliably removes slugs or snails.

ailments.name: Nitrogen deficiency
ailments.description: General pale growth, often beginning in older leaves, can suggest low nitrogen. Check: Check leaf age, growth, feeding history and root conditions; consider a soil or growing-medium test. First actions: Correct the cause and use an appropriate balanced feed if deficiency is supported. Similar-looking problems: Root stress; low light; natural ageing. These signs suggest possibilities, not a confirmed diagnosis.

ailments.description: A dark, sunken patch develops at the blossom end of susceptible fruit. Check: Inspect the location and review fluctuating soil moisture; this is a physiological disorder.
